text: They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
reflection: The first morning of a new year has a particular freshness to it. The calendar is clean, the pages are unwritten, and for a moment everything feels possible. Jeremiah wrote this verse at a very different kind of morning. Jerusalem lay in ruins, and he sat among the ashes of everything he had loved. Yet in the middle of his grief he remembered something that changed his outlook: "They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." God's mercies do not run on last year's supply. They are renewed with every sunrise. Whatever you carry into this year, whether regret, weariness, or uncertainty, you do not have to face it with yesterday's strength. There is fresh mercy waiting for you today, and there will be fresh mercy tomorrow. Begin this year by looking up rather than back. The God who carried you through every morning of last year has not changed. His faithfulness is great, and it is new again today.
question: What are you carrying into this new year that needs God's fresh mercy today?
prayer: Lord, Your mercies are new every morning, and great is Your faithfulness. I bring You what I carry into this year. Meet me with fresh mercy for today. Amen.

text: But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
reflection: Most of us start a new year with a list. We want to exercise more, spend less, read more, and worry less. Lists are not wrong, but Jesus offers a better starting point: "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you." He spoke these words to people who were anxious about food and clothing, the most basic needs of life. He did not say those needs were unimportant. He said they belonged in their proper place. When God's kingdom comes first, everything else finds its order. Our priorities settle, our worries shrink, and our hearts become steady. Seeking first means giving God the first thought of the morning, the first say in our decisions, and the first claim on our loyalty. Before you finalize your plans for this year, put Him at the top of the list. Then trust Him with everything below it. He knows what you need.
question: What would change in your plans this year if God's kingdom truly came first?
prayer: Father, I want to seek Your kingdom and Your righteousness first. Take the top place in my plans this year, and help me trust You with everything that follows. Amen.

text: And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.
reflection: God spoke these words to people living far from home. The Israelites had been carried away to Babylon, and many of them wondered whether God had forgotten them. Through Jeremiah, He gave them a promise: "And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart." Notice the condition. God is not hiding from us, but He does invite wholehearted seeking. A half-hearted search rarely finds anything of value. We look for lost keys with determination. We search for answers to problems with focus and energy. God invites that same earnestness in our pursuit of Him. Wholehearted seeking might look like turning off a screen to pray, opening the Bible when you would rather scroll, or asking honest questions instead of drifting. The promise is that you will find Him. Not a distant idea of God, but God Himself. Bring your whole heart to Him today, and expect to be found.
question: What is one way you could seek God with your whole heart today?
prayer: Lord, You promised to be found by those who search for You with all their heart. I do not want to seek You halfway. Draw my whole heart to You today. Amen.

text: One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple.
reflection: If you could ask God for only one thing, what would it be? David answered that question in Psalm 27: "One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life." David was a king with armies, wealth, and enemies to defeat. He could have asked for victory, security, or a longer reign. Instead, his deepest desire was to be near God and to behold His beauty. That single desire simplified his life. When we want many things equally, we are pulled in many directions. When one desire rises above the rest, the others begin to fall into line. Being close to God is not a reward for finishing everything else. It is the center that holds everything else together. Today, let your many wants become one. Ask to know God more, to see His beauty, and to stay near Him all your days.
question: If you could ask God for only one thing, what would it be, and why?
prayer: Lord, let my one desire be to dwell near You and behold Your beauty. Gather my scattered wants into that one longing, and keep me close to You all my days. Amen.

text: O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is…
reflection: David wrote Psalm 63 in the wilderness of Judah, a dry and dusty place where water was scarce. He knew real thirst, the kind that makes the mouth parched and the body weak. And he used that experience to describe his longing for God: "O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee." Thirst is not a polite preference. It is an urgent need that will not go away until it is satisfied. David recognized that his soul had the same kind of need. Nothing else could quench it but God Himself. Sometimes we try to satisfy our soul's thirst with busyness, entertainment, approval, or possessions. They may help for a moment, but the dryness returns. Only God truly satisfies. Notice also that David sought God early. He did not wait until the day was spent. Bring your thirst to God this morning. He is the living water your soul has been looking for.
question: What dry place in your soul have you been trying to satisfy with something other than God?
prayer: O God, You are my God, and my soul thirsts for You. Forgive me for chasing what cannot satisfy. Refresh my dry places this morning with Yourself. Amen.

text: But if from thence thou shalt seek the LORD thy God, thou shalt find him, if thou seek him with all thy heart and with all thy soul.
reflection: Moses spoke these words to a people who had not yet entered the Promised Land. Looking ahead, he warned them that they might one day turn away from God and end up scattered among other nations. But even in that warning, he left the door open: "But if from thence thou shalt seek the LORD thy God, thou shalt find him." From thence. From wherever you have ended up. From the far country of your own choices. From the place you never expected to be. God does not wait for us to fix everything before we come back. He invites us to seek Him from right where we are. Perhaps you feel far from God today. Maybe you drifted slowly, or maybe you walked away on purpose. Either way, the promise stands. Seek Him with all your heart and soul, and you will find Him. No distance is too great for a God who wants to be found.
question: What would it look like to seek God from right where you are today, without waiting to fix everything first?
prayer: Lord, I do not have to be in a better place to seek You. I seek You from right here, just as I am. Thank You that You are found by those who look for You. Amen.

text: As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.
reflection: Picture a deer in a dry season, searching for a stream. It is not wandering casually. It is driven by need, moving from place to place until it finds water. The psalmist used that picture to describe his soul: "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God." This psalm was written by someone who felt far from God. He remembered better days, when he had walked with the crowds to worship. Now he was downcast and longing. His honesty is a gift to us. Spiritual longing is not a sign that something is wrong with your faith. Often it is a sign that your faith is alive. A heart that pants for God is a heart that knows where real refreshment is found. If you feel dry today, do not hide it. Tell God you long for Him. Then go to the stream. Read His Word, pray, and wait for Him to refresh your soul.
question: What longing in your heart could you bring honestly to God today?
prayer: Lord, as the hart pants after the water brooks, so my soul pants after You. I bring You my thirst without pretending. Refresh me with Your living presence. Amen.

text: Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
reflection: Our minds can be restless places. Thoughts race ahead to tomorrow's problems, replay yesterday's conversations, and invent worries that may never happen. Isaiah offers a different way: "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee." The word stayed means propped up, leaning, supported. A mind stayed on God is a mind that rests its full weight on Him. It is not a mind that never thinks about problems, but a mind that keeps returning to Him in the middle of them. Perfect peace is not the absence of trouble. It is the steady calm of a heart that trusts. This peace does not depend on how well your day goes. It depends on where your thoughts are anchored. Today, when your mind begins to spin, gently bring it back. Remind yourself who God is and what He has promised. Lean your whole weight on Him.
question: When your thoughts start to spin today, what truth about God could you lean your mind on?
prayer: Lord, keep me in perfect peace as my mind stays on You. When my thoughts begin to race, turn them back to You, and steady my heart with trust. Amen.

text: Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before…
reflection: The apostle Paul had plenty in his past that could have held him back. Before he followed Christ, he persecuted believers. After he followed Christ, he suffered beatings, shipwrecks, and prison. He also had remarkable successes. Yet he wrote, "this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before." Paul was not pretending the past did not happen. He was refusing to let it steer his future. Both failures and achievements can become anchors. Old guilt can whisper that you are disqualified. Old victories can tempt you to coast. Paul let go of both. He leaned forward like a runner straining toward the finish. As this year unfolds, what from the past is still pulling at you? Bring it to God. Receive His forgiveness for what was wrong and give Him thanks for what was good. Then turn your face forward. There is more ahead than behind.
question: Is there an old guilt or an old success that is still steering you, and can you leave it with God?
prayer: Lord, I give You my past, both the failures that shame me and the victories I lean on. Help me forget what is behind and reach forward to what You have prepared. Amen.

text: I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
reflection: Paul continued his thought with a picture from the athletic games of his day: "I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus." A runner in a race does not wander. Eyes fixed on the finish line, every step is purposeful. Paul saw his whole life that way. He was not drifting through the years. He was pressing toward something. The prize he sought was not a trophy or a title. It was the high calling of God, the full purpose God had for him in Christ. That calling was worth every ounce of effort. We can easily drift through a year without direction. Days blur together, and we look up in December wondering where the time went. Pressing toward the mark means living on purpose. It means asking each day what God is calling you toward and taking steps in that direction. Keep your eyes on the prize today. Run with purpose.
question: What is one step you could take today toward what God is calling you to?
prayer: Father, I press toward the mark for the prize of Your high calling in Christ Jesus. Give me purpose and endurance today, and keep my eyes on the finish line. Amen.

text: Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
reflection: God spoke these words to a people who were stuck in the past. They kept looking back at the great things God had done, like the parting of the Red Sea, and wondering if anything like that could ever happen again. God's answer was startling: "Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it?" He was not finished. He would make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert. Deserts and wildernesses are places where roads and rivers do not naturally exist. That is exactly where God promised to work. Perhaps a part of your life feels like a wilderness right now. You cannot see a path forward, and everything feels dry. God specializes in making roads where there are none and bringing water to dry ground. Do not assume that His best work is behind you. Look for the new thing He is doing. It may already be springing up.
question: Where might God already be doing a new thing in your life that you have not noticed?
prayer: Lord, You make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert. Open my eyes to the new thing You are doing, and help me stop looking only behind me. Amen.

text: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
reflection: Moses wrote Psalm 90, and it is one of the oldest prayers in the Bible. He had watched a whole generation pass away in the wilderness, and he knew how short human life is. So he prayed, "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." Numbering our days does not mean living in fear of death. It means living with an honest awareness that our time is limited and valuable. When we forget that, we waste days on things that do not matter and postpone the things that do. When we remember it, we become wiser. We say the kind word now. We forgive sooner. We spend more time with God and with the people we love. A new year is a good time to pray this prayer. Ask God to help you see your days clearly. Then invest them in what lasts. Each day is a gift worth spending well.
question: If you numbered your days honestly, what would you spend more of today on?
prayer: Lord, teach me to number my days, that I may apply my heart to wisdom. Help me spend today on what truly lasts and let go of what does not matter. Amen.

text: Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established.
reflection: At the start of a year, many of us have plans: projects to begin, goals to reach, problems to solve. Proverbs gives simple advice about all of it: "Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established." The word commit carries the idea of rolling something onto someone else. Picture a heavy load you can no longer carry, rolled onto stronger shoulders. That is what God invites you to do with your work. Committing your works to the Lord means bringing your plans to Him before you start, asking for His direction, and trusting Him with the outcome. It does not mean you stop working. It means you stop carrying the weight alone. And the promise is that your thoughts will be established. Your mind becomes steady. The anxious second-guessing quiets down. Before you dive into today's work, pause and roll it onto Him. Then work with a settled heart.
question: What piece of today's work could you consciously place in God's hands before you begin?
prayer: Lord, I commit my work to You before it begins. Settle my thoughts, steady my hands, and let what I do today be established by You. Amen.

text: Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass.
reflection: David wrote Psalm 37 as an older man, after a lifetime of seeing how things turn out. One of his conclusions was this: "Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass." Yesterday we thought about committing our works. Today the focus is wider: our way, the whole direction of our lives. Some decisions are too big for us to see clearly. Where to live, what work to pursue, how to handle a difficult relationship. We can feel paralyzed, afraid of choosing wrong. David's counsel is to hand the entire path to God and then trust Him. Trust is the key word. Committing without trusting is like giving someone your keys and then grabbing them back. True commitment lets go. And the promise is beautiful: He shall bring it to pass. God is able to accomplish what we cannot. Commit your way to Him today and rest in His faithfulness.
question: What part of your life have you committed to God but quietly taken back?
prayer: Lord, I commit my way to You and choose to trust You with it. When I am tempted to take the load back, remind me that You will bring it to pass. Amen.

text: Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.
reflection: This is one of the most loved promises in the Psalms: "Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart." It is easy to read it backward, as if God were promising to hand us whatever we want if we act religious enough. But the order matters. Delight comes first. When we truly delight in God, enjoying Him, treasuring Him, finding our gladness in Him, our desires begin to change. We start wanting what He wants. Our hearts align with His. Then the desires He fulfills are the very desires He has shaped. Delighting in God is not a duty to get through. It is a joy to discover. It might mean noticing His goodness in creation, savoring a verse that speaks to you, or simply resting in the knowledge that you are loved. Look for something to delight in about God today. Let Him become your joy, and watch your desires become more like His.
question: What is one reason you could enjoy God today, not just obey Him?
prayer: Lord, I want to delight in You, not only serve You. Shape the desires of my heart as I enjoy Your goodness, until what I want is what You want. Amen.

text: And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.
reflection: The day before this verse was a full one. Jesus had taught in the synagogue, cast out an unclean spirit, healed Peter's mother-in-law, and then, as evening came, healed many sick people while the whole city gathered at the door. He must have been exhausted. Yet the next morning we read, "rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed." Jesus did not pray because He had nothing else to do. He prayed because He had so much to do. Time alone with the Father was the source of His strength and direction. If Jesus needed that time, how much more do we? A solitary place does not have to be a mountain. It can be a quiet corner, a parked car, or a chair before the house wakes up. What matters is that you meet with God before the demands of the day crowd in. Find your quiet place today.
question: Where could you find a quiet place to meet with God before today's demands begin?
prayer: Lord Jesus, even You rose early to pray alone. Teach me to seek the Father before the noise of the day, and let my strength come from time with Him. Amen.

text: My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up.
reflection: David had a morning habit: "My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up." Notice the three parts of his prayer. First, he spoke to God. Second, he directed his prayer, arranging it carefully the way a priest laid out a sacrifice on the altar. Third, he looked up, watching expectantly for God's answer. Many of us do the first part and skip the rest. We say a quick prayer and then rush on, never looking for what God will do. David prayed with expectation. He believed God heard and would respond. That changed how he walked through the rest of his day. He was looking for God's hand. Try David's pattern this morning. Speak honestly to God. Bring your requests with care. Then look up. Go through your day watching for His answers, His help, and His presence. You may be surprised at how much you notice.
question: What prayer could you bring to God this morning and then watch expectantly for His answer?
prayer: Lord, in the morning I direct my prayer to You and look up. Give me eyes to see Your hand at work today, and a heart that expects You to answer. Amen.

text: Then shall we know, if we follow on to know the LORD: his going forth is prepared as the morning; and he shall come unto us as the rain, as the latter and former rain unto the earth.
reflection: Hosea lived in a time when people treated God casually. They would turn to Him in a crisis and forget Him when things improved. Hosea called them to something deeper: "Then shall we know, if we follow on to know the LORD." To follow on means to keep pursuing, to keep pressing in. Knowing God is not a single event. It is a lifelong pursuit. And Hosea paints a beautiful picture of what we find as we keep seeking: "his going forth is prepared as the morning; and he shall come unto us as the rain." The sunrise is certain. The rain refreshes dry ground. God is just as dependable, and just as life-giving. Do not settle for knowing about God from a distance. Keep following on. Keep reading, praying, listening, and obeying. Over time, your knowledge of Him will grow deeper, and His presence will become as familiar and welcome as the morning light.
question: What could you do today to press on in knowing God, not just knowing about Him?
prayer: Lord, I want to follow on to know You. Your coming is as sure as the morning and as refreshing as the rain. Draw me deeper into knowing You today. Amen.

text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and rain righteousness upon you.
reflection: Farmers understand fallow ground. It is soil that has been left unplowed. Over time it becomes hard, packed, and covered with weeds. Nothing new can grow there until it is broken up. Hosea used that image to speak to hearts: "break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and rain righteousness upon you." A heart can become fallow too. Not through dramatic rebellion, but through neglect. Prayer becomes rare. Scripture goes unread. Spiritual things grow hard and dry. Breaking up fallow ground is hard work, but it prepares the soil to receive rain. Perhaps there is an area of your life that has gone unplowed for a while. A habit you have let slide. A relationship you have neglected. A sin you have stopped noticing. Today is the time to seek the Lord. Let Him break up what has hardened, and get ready for the rain of His righteousness.
question: Where has your heart grown hard from neglect, and how could you break up that ground today?
prayer: Lord, break up the fallow ground of my heart. Soften what neglect has hardened, and prepare me to receive Your rain of righteousness. It is time to seek You. Amen.

text: For thus saith the LORD unto the house of Israel, Seek ye me, and ye shall live…
reflection: Amos was a farmer and shepherd whom God called to speak to a prosperous but unfaithful nation. The people were busy with religious ceremonies, but their hearts were far from God. Into that noise came a simple message: "Seek ye me, and ye shall live." Notice what God did not say. He did not say, seek more rituals, or seek more activity. He said, seek Me. The invitation was personal. God wanted His people, not just their performances. And the promise was life. Real life, not mere existence. It is possible to be busy with good things and still miss God. We can attend events, sing songs, and post verses while our hearts drift. Amos calls us back to the center. Today, set aside the busyness for a moment and seek God Himself. Talk to Him, listen to Him, and enjoy Him. That is where life is found.
question: Is your walk with God more activity than relationship right now, and how could you seek Him personally today?
prayer: Lord, I do not want only to be busy for You. I want to know You. Help me seek You Yourself today, and find the life You promise. Amen.

text: Seek ye the LORD, all ye meek of the earth, which have wrought his judgment; seek righteousness, seek meekness: it may be ye shall be hid in the day of the LORD'S anger.
reflection: Zephaniah spoke during a time of warning. Judgment was coming, and the people needed to turn. His call went out especially to the humble: "Seek ye the LORD, all ye meek of the earth." And then he added, "seek righteousness, seek meekness." It is interesting that he told the meek to seek meekness. Humility is never something we finish. Even those who are humble need to keep pursuing it, because pride is always ready to creep back in. Meekness is not weakness. It is strength under control, a heart that bows before God and treats others gently. Righteousness is doing what is right in God's eyes. Together they describe a person who lives close to God. In a world that praises self-promotion, God values a meek and righteous heart. Today, seek the Lord with humility. Ask Him to show you where pride has taken root. Let Him shape you into someone gentle, upright, and near to Him.
question: Where do you most need God to make you more gentle and humble today?
prayer: Lord, I seek You, Your righteousness, and meekness. Humility does not come once for all, so keep working it into me. Make me gentle, upright, and close to You. Amen.

text: Seek the LORD and his strength, seek his face continually.
reflection: King David brought the ark of God to Jerusalem with great celebration. Afterward, he gave the people a song of thanks, and in the middle of it was this line: "Seek the LORD and his strength, seek his face continually." Three things to seek. The Lord Himself, His strength, and His face. Seeking His strength means relying on His power rather than our own. Seeking His face means desiring His presence and His favor, the warmth of being near Him. And the word continually means this is not a once-in-a-while activity. It is a lifestyle. You can seek God's face while you drive, cook, work, or wait. A quick prayer, a whispered thanks, a moment of remembering He is near. These small turnings of the heart add up to a life lived in His presence. Today, look for moments to turn your face toward His. Seek Him not only in the quiet hour, but continually.
question: What moments in your ordinary day could become reminders to turn your heart toward God?
prayer: Lord, I want to seek Your face continually, not only now and then. Turn my heart toward You again and again through this day, in the small moments as well as the large. Amen.

text: If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
reflection: After Solomon dedicated the temple, God appeared to him at night with a promise that has encouraged people for centuries: "If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land." Notice that the call is to God's own people. Before pointing at others, God asks those who bear His name to look inward. There are four steps: humble yourselves, pray, seek His face, and turn from wickedness. And there are three promises: He will hear, He will forgive, and He will heal. Healing begins with humility. When we stop defending ourselves and come honestly before God, He responds with mercy. Today, take the first step. Humble yourself before Him. Pray honestly. Seek His face. Turn from anything you know is wrong. Then trust Him to hear, forgive, and heal.
question: What step of humility could you take before God today?
prayer: Lord, I humble myself before You. Show me where I need to turn, and hear me as I pray and seek Your face. Forgive, and bring Your healing to my life. Amen.

text: And they that know thy name will put their trust in thee: for thou, LORD, hast not forsaken them that seek thee.
reflection: Trust is built on knowledge. We trust people whose character we have come to know. David understood this when he wrote, "And they that know thy name will put their trust in thee: for thou, LORD, hast not forsaken them that seek thee." In the Bible, a name is more than a label. It reveals character. To know God's name is to know who He is: faithful, merciful, just, and strong. The more we learn of Him, the easier it becomes to trust Him. And David adds a reason grounded in experience. God has never forsaken those who seek Him. Not once. Throughout history, people who turned to Him found that He was there. If trusting God feels hard today, perhaps the answer is to get to know Him better. Read about His faithfulness in Scripture. Remember what He has done in your own life. As you know His name more deeply, your trust will grow stronger.
question: What do you know about God's character that helps you trust Him today?
prayer: Lord, those who know Your name will put their trust in You, for You have not forsaken those who seek You. Help me know You better, so my trust in You grows. Amen.

text: The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing.
reflection: Young lions are among the strongest hunters in the animal world. They are fast, powerful, and fierce. Yet David observed something surprising: "The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing." Strength does not guarantee provision. Even the mightiest creatures go hungry sometimes. But those who seek the Lord have a different source. God Himself becomes their supply. This does not mean that God's people never face hardship. David himself wrote this psalm after a frightening escape from a foreign king. But it does mean that God will not withhold any truly good thing from those who seek Him. If He keeps something from you, it is because it is not good for you, or not good yet. Today, release your grip on your own strength and seek the Lord. Trust that He knows what is good, and that He will not let you lack it.
question: What need are you trying to meet in your own strength that you could trust God to supply?
prayer: Father, even strong lions go hungry, but those who seek You lack no good thing. I stop relying on my own strength and trust You to supply what is truly good. Amen.

text: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.
reflection: Martha welcomed Jesus into her house and threw herself into preparing a good meal. Her sister Mary, meanwhile, was sitting at His feet, listening. Frustrated, Martha asked Jesus to tell Mary to help. His answer was gentle but clear: "But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her." Jesus did not criticize Martha's service. He loved her. But He saw that she was distracted and troubled about many things. Mary had chosen something better: time in His presence, hearing His words. That choice would never be taken from her. Our lives are often more like Martha's. Work, family, and responsibilities crowd our days, and good things squeeze out the best thing. Mary's example reminds us to make room for sitting at Jesus' feet. It is a choice, and sometimes it means leaving other things undone for a while. Choose the good part today.
question: What good activity has been crowding out time at Jesus' feet?
prayer: Lord Jesus, like Mary, I want to choose the good part. Quiet my busy heart, help me sit at Your feet today, and let me listen to Your word. Amen.

text: And I say unto you, Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
reflection: Jesus told a story about a man who knocked on his friend's door at midnight to borrow bread. The friend did not want to get up, but the man kept knocking until he did. Then Jesus said, "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." The three verbs grow in intensity. Asking uses your voice. Seeking uses your whole attention. Knocking uses persistence, refusing to give up. Jesus was teaching us to pray with that kind of earnestness. Not because God is reluctant like the sleepy friend, but because persistent prayer shapes us and shows how much we truly want what we ask. God is a loving Father who delights to give good gifts. He is not annoyed by our asking. He invites it. Is there something you stopped praying about because the answer seemed slow? Pick it up again today. Ask, seek, and keep knocking.
question: What prayer have you set down that you could pick up and keep knocking on today?
prayer: Father, You told us to ask, seek, and knock. I bring back the prayer I had set aside, trusting that You are a loving Father who hears. Amen.

text: If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God.
reflection: Paul wrote to believers in Colosse that they had been raised with Christ into a new life. Because of that, their focus needed to change: "If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God." Our attention naturally goes to what is right in front of us: bills, schedules, news, and the opinions of others. These things are real, but they are not ultimate. Paul invites us to lift our eyes. Christ is seated at the right hand of God, reigning in power. His kingdom, His purposes, and His values are the things above. Seeking those things means letting heaven's priorities shape our earthly choices. It means asking what matters to Christ and pursuing that. This changes how we handle money, relationships, conflict, and success. Today, before you get lost in the urgent, lift your eyes. Seek the things above, where Christ is.
question: Which choice today could be shaped by heaven's priorities instead of earth's?
prayer: Lord, I have been raised with Christ, so help me seek those things which are above. Let heaven's priorities shape my choices, my time, and my words today. Amen.

text: Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.
reflection: Paul followed his call to seek things above with a related instruction: "Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth." The word affection here refers to the mind and its focus. Seeking is about what we pursue. Setting our affection is about what we think about and care for. Our thoughts are like a compass needle. They tend to swing toward whatever we love most. If our minds are always on possessions, status, or comfort, those things will steer our lives. If our minds are set on God, His goodness will steer us instead. Setting our affection is an intentional act. It does not happen by accident. It means choosing what we feed our minds with, what we dwell on, and what we allow to shape our desires. Today, take inventory of your thoughts. Where does your mind naturally drift? Then gently set it again on things above.
question: What has been filling your mind lately, and how could you set it on things above today?
prayer: Lord, I set my affection on things above, not on things on the earth. Where my thoughts have drifted, draw them back to You and to Your goodness. Amen.

text: With my whole heart have I sought thee: O let me not wander from thy commandments.
reflection: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, and nearly every verse speaks of God's Word. In this early verse, the psalmist makes a confession and a request: "With my whole heart have I sought thee: O let me not wander from thy commandments." He has sought God sincerely. Yet he knows he could still wander. Even a wholehearted seeker is not immune to drifting. That honesty is refreshing. Some of the most sincere believers are also the most aware of their weakness. They do not trust their own steadiness. They ask God to keep them. This is a wise prayer for any season. We can start well and still drift. We can be passionate today and distracted tomorrow. The psalmist's answer is to cling to God's commandments, His Word, as a guardrail on the road. Pray this prayer today. Tell God you are seeking Him, and ask Him to keep you from wandering.
question: Where are you most likely to wander from God's ways, and how could you ask Him to keep you?
prayer: Lord, with my whole heart I have sought You. O let me not wander from Your commandments. Keep me close to Your Word and on Your path today. Amen.

text: I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.
reflection: As the first month of the year comes to a close, here is a verse to carry into the rest of it: "I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved." David made a decision. He set the Lord before him. Like setting a picture on a desk where you will see it all day, he kept God in view. And because God was at his right hand, the place of a protector and helper, David was steady. He would not be shaken. Many things try to move us. Bad news, criticism, temptation, disappointment, and fear all push against our footing. What keeps us steady is not our own strength but the nearness of God. When He is before us and beside us, we can stand firm. This month we have thought about seeking God first. Now make it a lasting habit. Set Him before you every day, and you will not be moved.
question: How could you keep the Lord before you through every day of this year?
prayer: Lord, I set You always before me. Because You are at my right hand, I shall not be moved. Help me keep You in view through every day of this year. Amen.
